title: Communication in co-located, remote and hybrid teams
blurb: Explain how communication must be handled when an agile team sits together, works remotely, or mixes both.
question: At Callowmere University, some wellbeing staff are on campus and others work part-time or remotely, and they often miss decisions made face to face. How should communication be handled for this team?

teach.body: Good communication avoids misconceptions and needless barriers to change. In agile work, short iterations and shifting priorities leave little time for misunderstanding, so agile favours rich communication: words plus visuals, conversation and body language. Communication also flows both ways: people must be heard as well as told. Where the team sits, together, apart or both, changes how much of this happens naturally and how much must be planned.

Agreed in initiating a project, it defines the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, across the project ecosystem. It sets up a controlled, bidirectional flow and is as much about listening as broadcasting: understand people's concerns and address them before they become bigger risks, and tailor messages to each group. Generic messages rarely work; key influencers from user, supplier and business groups help tailor them.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4, Tables 4.1 and 13.6

head: Weak habit
PRINCE2 Agile habit
rows: Reports can be biased: add other feedback
Listen as much as you broadcast
teach.caption: Most communication in organizations happens outside formal channels: accept it and feed it.

teach.h: Three ways a team can sit
teach.caption: Parts a, b and c of the syllabus criterion: the exam asks which handling fits which setting.

teach.body: Co-located (a): people sitting together get rich communication naturally, and relationships grow in unstructured moments; visual boards and dashboards keep work visible. Remote (b): this does not happen by itself, so a more deliberate, structured approach is needed. Focus on clarity about how information flows through the ecosystem, information in appropriate formats, identifying key relationships, and agreeing both structured and unstructured time together.

teach.h: Setting up a remote team's communication

steps.label: Map the flow
steps.sub: How does information travel, and to whom?

steps.label: Pick formats
steps.sub: Ones people can find, share and reuse

teach.body: Hybrid (c) mixes people together and people apart. In plain English, the risk is a two-speed team: those in the room share rich, informal talk while remote members miss it. So apply the remote focus to the whole team: make information flow explicit, share it in formats everyone can reach, and plan time together. The book suggests that virtual, distant or hybrid teams may need extra activities, such as syncing co-location days for key people and teams.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Callowmere Student Support Hub (AS2)
teach.body: Wellbeing staff work across two campuses, some part-time or remotely, and keep missing face-to-face meetings. Project manager Jamal Hussain treats the team as hybrid. In the communication management approach he sets out where decisions are posted, short recorded demos staff can share, an open drop-in call with time for informal chat, an anonymous feedback form, and synced on-campus days for key people. He works with respected adviser Tom Brierley to tailor messages for doubtful colleagues.

teach.text: Classic traps: periodic reporting alone is NOT enough to judge a change, because reports can be biased towards what seems acceptable. Remote teams need structure AND unstructured time, not structure alone. And the communication management approach is not where agile behaviours are documented: that is the quality management approach.

items: Communication management approach: means and frequency of communication and feedback (4.4).
Bidirectional, listening as much as broadcasting; tailor messages via key influencers.
Co-located: rich communication and relationships grow naturally.
Remote: deliberate structure, clear information flow, formats, key relationships, structured and unstructured time.
Hybrid: make flow explicit for everyone; sync co-location days for key people.
Periodic reports alone are insufficient and can be biased.

summary: You can now explain how communication must be handled for co-located, remote and hybrid agile teams, and use the communication management approach to keep information flowing both ways. You can also spot the weak habits the exam uses as distractors: generic messages, formal channels alone and reliance on periodic reports.

A.q: At Callowmere, Northmere Systems' developers work fully remotely from another city. Decisions agreed by the on-campus web team often reach them days late or not in a usable form. Which approach BEST fits the guidance for remote teams?
options: Send Northmere the monthly highlight report for all decisions
Require Northmere's developers to work on campus each day
Agree how information flows and the formats it is shared in
Limit joint calls to a structured agenda of decision items
A.why: Remote teams need a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows through the ecosystem and information in appropriate formats (4.4).

whyNot.0: Periodic reports arrive too late for daily work and are not enough on their own.
whyNot.1: Mandating co-location is unlikely to be effective and does not fix the information flow.
whyNot.3: Remote teams need structured AND unstructured time together, not agenda items alone.

A.q: Pinewick's e-commerce team of eight sits together at head office with a shared board on the wall. A new project manager asks why this setting helps the team's communication. Which explanation is BEST?
options: Rich face-to-face talk; relationships grow in informal moments
The team needs no communication management approach of its own
The shared wall board removes the need for a team dashboard
The team can rely on periodic written reports to stay aligned
A.why: Co-located teams get rich communication (words, visuals, body language) and build relationships organically in unstructured moments (2.7.3, 4.3.3).

whyNot.1: The communication management approach covers the whole ecosystem, whatever the team setting.
whyNot.2: A wall board can BE the team dashboard; co-location does not remove the need for visibility.
whyNot.3: Periodic reporting alone is insufficient in any setting (4.4).

A.q: At Larkspur Rail, the project manager plans one monthly newsletter, sent to passengers, customer relations staff, Coinbridge and the board, to explain the Fair Fares changes. Which improvement BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile communication guidance?
options: Send the newsletter weekly so that every group hears more often
Make the newsletter longer so it covers every group's concerns
Ask each group to reply through the formal complaints channel
Tailor messages for each group through its key influencers
A.why: Generic messaging is rarely effective; working with key influencers from the user, supplier and business groups allows tailored messages and strong feedback loops (4.4).

whyNot.0: More frequent generic messages are still generic.
whyNot.1: A longer single message is still one message for all groups.
whyNot.2: Feedback should come through multiple pathways, not one formal channel.

B.q: Callowmere's wellbeing staff are split: some work on campus, others part-time or from home. Decisions about the new triage process are often made in corridor conversations on campus, and remote staff find out late. Which action BEST fits the guidance for this hybrid team?
options: Hold all decisions until the monthly staff meeting on campus
Make the flow of decisions explicit and shareable for all staff
Ask remote staff to come to campus whenever a decision is due
Leave news to spread through informal corridor conversations
B.why: In a hybrid team the remote focus applies: clarity on how information flows, in formats people can share, so remote members are not left behind (4.4).

whyNot.0: Delaying decisions to a monthly meeting slows the work and still excludes part-time staff.
whyNot.2: Mandating attendance is unlikely to work and ignores why staff work remotely.
whyNot.3: Informal channels should be accepted and fed, but on their own they leave remote staff out.

B.q: At Easterholm County Council, the programme board chair wants monthly written reports and no dashboards. The project manager plans to judge how well social workers are adopting Care Online from these reports alone. Why does PRINCE2 Agile advise against this?
options: Reports alone can be biased towards what seems acceptable
Written reports are not used in PRINCE2 Agile projects
Highlight reports must be produced weekly in agile projects
Monthly reports exceed the board's reporting tolerance
B.why: Relying on periodic reporting to assess a change is insufficient; people may adjust what they report to what is acceptable, expected or desirable (4.4).

whyNot.1: Written reports can be used; the project dashboard tailors the highlight report, but reporting is not banned.
whyNot.2: PRINCE2 Agile sets no weekly frequency for highlight reports.
whyNot.3: Tolerances apply to performance aspects, not to how often reports are sent.

B.q: Saltmarsh's project manager is drafting the communication management approach for Repairs Reimagined. Which content BEST reflects its purpose?
options: The agile behaviours expected of each team member
The target state for agile ways of working at Saltmarsh
The means and frequency of communication and feedback
Who decides and who advises in each decision area
B.why: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, across the ecosystem (4.4, Table 4.1).

whyNot.0: Agile behaviours are documented in the quality management approach.
whyNot.1: The target state belongs in the change management approach.
whyNot.3: Decision rights per area belong in a delegation matrix.

C.q: For Callowmere's hybrid wellbeing team, the project manager posts every decision and a short recorded demo on a shared online space, runs an open drop-in call with time for informal chat, offers an anonymous feedback form, and syncs on-campus days for key people. Is this an appropriate way to handle communication, and why?
options: Yes, because recorded demos can replace face-to-face contact
Yes, because it makes flow explicit and opens many feedback paths
No, because feedback should come through formal channels
No, because a hybrid team should meet in person for decisions
C.why: Hybrid teams need the remote focus applied to everyone: clear information flow, shareable formats, multiple feedback paths and time together, including synced co-location days for key people (4.4, 4.3.3).

whyNot.0: The plan still includes synced in-person days; recordings support contact, they do not replace it.
whyNot.2: Most communication happens outside formal channels; offering several pathways is the guidance.
whyNot.3: Requiring in-person decisions excludes part-time and remote staff.

C.q: At Larkspur, Coinbridge Payments' team works remotely. To keep things efficient, the project manager limits contact with them to a weekly structured status call with a fixed agenda. Is this an appropriate way to communicate with a remote team, and why?
options: Yes, because remote teams need a deliberate, structured approach
Yes, because a fixed-price supplier is managed through its contract
No, because remote teams also need key links and unstructured time
No, because a remote supplier team should be co-located for the work
C.why: For remote teams, the focus includes identifying key relationships and agreeing both structured and unstructured time together (4.4). A single structured call does not do that.

whyNot.0: True that remote teams need structure, but structure alone is not enough, so the verdict is wrong.
whyNot.1: The contract governs the commercial relationship, not day-to-day communication.
whyNot.3: Co-location is not required; remote teams can work well with deliberate communication.

C.q: At Easterholm, the project manager plans to judge whether front door staff are adopting the new online assessments from the monthly written highlight report, with no other feedback routes. Is this an appropriate approach to communication, and why?
options: Yes, because the board chair has asked to receive written reports
Yes, because highlight reports are the PRINCE2 progress product
No, because reports should go to the agile coach, not the board
No, because periodic reports alone may be biased and insufficient
C.why: It is insufficient to rely on periodic reporting alone to assess a change; reports can be biased, so offer multiple feedback paths and listen directly (4.4).

whyNot.0: The chair's preference does not make reports enough to understand adoption.
whyNot.1: True that highlight reports report progress, but they do not explain why this plan is acceptable.
whyNot.2: Reports still go to the board; the flaw is relying on them alone.

reteach.title: Same office, different time zones, or both
reteach.question: Think of a family planning a holiday: everyone at the kitchen table, everyone on a group call, or half and half. What changes?

blocks.h: Kitchen table, group call, half and half
blocks.body: Round the kitchen table, ideas, jokes and frowns flow freely: that is co-located. On a group call, someone has to share the itinerary, check everyone can open it, and leave time to chat: that is remote. Half and half is the hardest: the people at the table must make sure the ones on the phone hear what was decided, and the family plans a few days together.

blocks.text: Structure alone is not enough for remote teams: they need unstructured time too. And a report is not a conversation.

explain.body: Sitting together gives rich communication: words, visuals, body language. Relationships grow in unstructured moments, and visual boards keep work visible.

test.q: Draycott's software team of five works side by side in one office. Which feature of this setting MOST helps their communication?
options: Written status notes replace conversations
Formal agendas replace informal discussions
Weekly reports replace the team dashboard
Rich, face-to-face talk in informal moments
test.why: Co-location supports rich communication and organic relationship building in unstructured activities (2.7.3, 4.3.3).

whyNot.0: Written notes are less rich than conversation; they are not the benefit of sitting together.
whyNot.1: Formal agendas make meetings efficient but do not build relationships.
whyNot.2: Periodic reports do not replace visible team information.

explain.body: Needs a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows, appropriate formats, identifying key relationships, and agreeing structured and unstructured time together.

test.q: Saltmarsh's three-person digital team works fully from home. Which approach BEST fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance for this remote team?
options: Rely on informal chat to pass on decisions
Agree flow, formats and time spent together
Hold one long monthly call to cover all work
Bring the team into the office every day
test.why: Remote teams need clarity on information flow and formats, key relationships, and both structured and unstructured time (4.4).

whyNot.0: Informal chat alone gives no deliberate structure for a remote team.
whyNot.2: A single monthly call gives little structure and almost no unstructured time.
whyNot.3: Mandating office attendance is unlikely to be effective.

explain.body: Some together, some apart. Make information flow explicit for everyone in shareable formats, and plan time together; virtual, distant or hybrid teams may need synced co-location days for key people and teams.

test.q: Pinewick's store operations team has two members at head office and three in stores. Store-based members say they hear about decisions late. Which action BEST fits a hybrid team?
options: Share decisions in a format all members can reach
Move the store-based members into head office
Let head office members take all the decisions
Report decisions in the monthly highlight report
test.why: In a hybrid team, information flow must be made explicit in formats everyone can reach, so remote members are not left behind (4.4).

whyNot.1: Mandating co-location is unlikely to work and takes people away from the stores.
whyNot.2: Centralizing decisions removes the store members' voice instead of fixing the flow.
whyNot.3: A monthly report is too slow and periodic reporting alone is insufficient.

explain.body: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication and feedback, two ways. Tailor messages through key influencers; accept informal channels and give shareable formats and many feedback paths.

test.q: Draycott's engineers mostly hear about the project through talk on the shop floor rather than official notices. How should the project manager respond?
options: Ask engineers to use official notices instead
Stop shop-floor talk about the project's work
Provide shareable material and feedback routes
Add more detail to the official monthly notice
test.why: Most communication happens outside formal channels; accept it, provide information in formats people can share, and offer multiple feedback paths (4.4).

whyNot.0: Pushing everyone to formal channels works against how people actually communicate.
whyNot.1: Suppressing informal talk loses an important channel for the change.
whyNot.3: A longer formal notice does not reach people where they actually talk.
